_fixture_requirements.note: The roster in tests/suite/README.md does not pin down what is in each fixture's name table, and the fonts tests/suite/fixtures/build.py currently produces do not carry the records this area needs. The `observed` block records what is in the fixtures today, read with fontTools 4.62.1; the `required_additions` block is what build.py must add before the cases that use those records can run. Nothing here asks for an existing string to change.

recursive-vf.source: testdata/fonts/Recursive-VF.subset.ttf, copied verbatim; not generated, so nothing here is a request
recursive-vf.platforms: every record is 3/1/1033; no Macintosh and no non-English records
recursive-vf.axes: MONO 0/0/1, CASL 0/0/1, wght 300/300/1000, slnt -15/0/0, CRSV 0/0.5/1; 64 named instances; STAT with five design axis records (269-273) and eleven axis values

two-axis.axes: wght 100/400/900, wdth 75/100/125; no fvar named instances; STAT on both axes; avar

named-instances.axes: wght 100/400/900, wdth 75/100/125; 8 named instances, the default one using subfamilyNameID 2; STAT with five wght values and three wdth values, Regular and Normal elidable

named-instances.what: 3/1/1033 records for the four optional family names
named-instances.why: Without these there is no fixture in the roster that has a name ID 16, 17, 21 or 22, and D5 — the corpus's largest suspected defect, that the original strips all four from every font it touches — cannot be tested at all. named-instances is the right home for them because with eight named instances it is an extended typographic family in the specification's sense, the case where IDs 16 and 17 are strongly recommended. The values are deliberately distinct from IDs 1 and 2 so a case can tell which record an implementation wrote.
named-instances.used_by: every names.d5.* case, and the D4 cases on this fixture

named-instances.why: No fixture currently has a record in any language other than English, so D2's 'only 3/1/1033 is read and written' cannot be tested against a non-English record, and there is nothing in any fixture that distinguishes reading 3/1/1033 from reading whatever record comes first. The two non-ASCII strings also give the corpus a UTF-16BE round trip through an existing record rather than through user input.

named-instances.what: a GSUB 'ss01' feature with FeatureParams UINameID 276, and a 3/1/1033 record 276 = “Alternate H”
named-instances.why: The G10 pruning rule is subtler than 'drop unused': fontTools removes only the IDs above 255 that fvar or STAT referenced before the slice and no longer do, so a name ID referenced from a layout feature is never a candidate even though no variation table points at it. No fixture currently has a FeatureParams name ID — recursive-vf's only GSUB feature is 'rvrn' with FeatureParams None — so this property has nothing to test against. A single substitution such as H to O is enough to hang the feature on. If the fixture owner would rather not add GSUB to this font, the case should move to whichever fixture gains a stylistic set rather than be dropped.
named-instances.used_by: names.g10.layout-feature-label-survives; also the ID 276 entry in names.g10.exact-surviving-name-ids-on-named-instances

_proposed_checks.passes_when: a record with that (platformID, encodingID, languageID, nameID) key exists and its decoded string equals `equals`
_proposed_checks.justification: The listed name_record kind is hard-wired to 3/1/1033. Claim D2 is precisely that only 3/1/1033 is read and written, and the only way to test the 'only' half is to assert what happened to records on other keys. The specification defines a record's identity as the full four-part key — 'name records must be sorted first by platform ID, then by platform-specific encoding ID, then by language ID, and then by name ID' — so a check that can address one key alone cannot describe what an edit did to the table.

_proposed_checks.passes_when: no record with that four-part key exists
_proposed_checks.justification: Needed to assert that an implementation did not invent records on platforms the editor never claimed to write. Since 'strings for the Macintosh platform (platform ID 1) use platform-specific single- or double-byte encodings', a tool that mirrored an edit onto platform 1 could not represent arbitrary user text there; a case has to be able to say the mirror did not happen.

_proposed_checks.passes_when: the number of records with that nameID, across all platforms, encodings and languages, equals `equals`
_proposed_checks.justification: Cheaper and more robust than enumerating every key when the property under test is 'editing one localisation neither duplicated nor deleted the others'. It is also the only way to catch an implementation that adds a second 3/1/1033 record for an ID instead of replacing the first, which the specification forbids for ID 17: the string 'must be unique within a particular typographic family'.

_proposed_checks.passes_when: the record's stored bytes are in the named encoding (utf_16_be, mac_roman, ...), as reported by fontTools NameRecord.getEncoding()
_proposed_checks.justification: The specification states that for the Windows platform, outside the code-page encodings 3, 4 and 5, 'all string data for platform 3 must be encoded in UTF-16BE'. A round trip through a decoder cannot distinguish a correctly encoded record from one a lenient decoder happened to recover; this asserts the bytes on disk, which is what the specification constrains.

_proposed_checks.passes_when: the compiled records appear in ascending order of (platformID, encodingID, languageID, nameID)
_proposed_checks.justification: Directly required: 'name records must be sorted first by platform ID, then by platform-specific encoding ID, then by language ID, and then by name ID.' A tool that appends edited records to the end of the array produces a table that violates this, and no listed check would notice. fontTools sorts on compile, so the original satisfies it for free; a reimplementation that writes its own name table does not.

_proposed_checks.passes_when: every nameID referenced from fvar (axisNameID, instance subfamilyNameID, instance postScriptNameID other than 0xFFFF), from STAT (AxisNameID, ValueNameID, ElidedFallbackNameID) and from GSUB/GPOS FeatureParams (UINameID and the stylistic-set and character-variant label IDs) has at least one matching record in the name table
_proposed_checks.justification: The listed no_dangling_name_ids check tests one direction — that no name record is orphaned — and counts only fvar and STAT as referrers. Two things it cannot see. First, a name ID above 255 referenced from GSUB FeatureParams is legitimate, since the specification reserves 'name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive ... for font-specific names such as those referenced by a font's layout features', so no_dangling_name_ids gives a false failure on any font with a stylistic-set label. Second, the opposite fault: a surviving fvar or STAT record pointing at a name record that an edit deleted, which is the failure clearing a name cell can actually cause, and which is reachable because fvar permits an instance's subfamilyNameID to be 2 or 17.

cases.title: All nine editable rows reach the output as 3/1/1033 records
cases.rationale: The editor exposes exactly nine name IDs — 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 16, 17, 21, 22 — and the name specification says of them that “the key information for this table for Microsoft platforms relates to the use of name IDs 1, 2, 4, 16 and 17” and that “fonts should include all of these strings for the broadest application compatibility”. A slicer that offered a row and then dropped what was typed into it would be worse than not offering the row. This is the baseline for the whole area: nine cells in, nine records out, each holding exactly the typed string.

cases.title: Editing all nine rows overwrites the records the font already had
cases.rationale: The previous case creates records that were absent; this one replaces records that were present, which is a different path in any implementation that treats 16, 17, 21 and 22 as optional. Name ID 17 “must be unique within a particular typographic family”, so an implementation that appended a second 3/1/1033 record instead of replacing the first would leave the table with two competing typographic subfamily names. Exactly one record per key must come out, which is why the case also counts them: two records for ID 17, the edited English one and the untouched German one.

cases.title: Name ID 5 is read-only, and records outside the nine are carried through
cases.rationale: The editor reads name ID 5 only to show a version in the status bar; there is no row for it, so the string must survive, and so must every other name ID outside the nine. The specification requires ID 5 to “begin with the pattern Version <number>.<number>” and notes that “the first such match in the string can be used by installation software to compare font versions”, so blanking or bumping it would change how installers treat the file. ID 0 is the vendor’s copyright notice, which no font tool has any business rewriting. The case edits five rows the editor does own, to show that doing so perturbs neither.

cases.title: Editing name ID 1 changes the 3/1/1033 record and no other
cases.rationale: The editor’s contract is one localisation: Windows, Unicode BMP, English (US). The specification blesses that key — “when building a Unicode font for Windows, the platform ID should be 3 and the encoding ID should be 1” — but it also treats every other record as an independent string in its own language and encoding, and a tool cannot translate the user’s text into German or re-encode it for Mac Roman. Writing the edit anywhere else would corrupt or mistranslate those records, so the Macintosh and German name ID 1 records must come out exactly as they went in, and there must still be three of them.

cases.title: A font with Macintosh platform records keeps every one of them
cases.rationale: Platform 1 records are a legitimate part of the table — the specification lists platform ID 1 as valid in the name table and notes that “many newer platforms can use strings intended for different platforms if a font does not include strings for that platform”. Nothing about narrowing a design space invalidates a Macintosh string, so all of the fixture’s Mac records must be present and unchanged after a full pin with the name editor untouched. The encoding check matters because “strings for the Macintosh platform (platform ID 1) use platform-specific single- or double-byte encodings”: a tool that rewrote them as UTF-16BE would leave records no consumer can read.

cases.title: German Windows records are preserved when the English ones are edited
cases.rationale: The name table exists to hold “multilingual strings”, and the specification’s whole design is that “later, the font can be localized and the strings translated or added”. A localisation is not derivable from the English string and cannot be regenerated, so losing one is unrecoverable. Editing the English family and subfamily must leave all four German records exactly as they were, including the two that carry U+00FC and U+00DC — characters that survive a UTF-16BE round trip but not a naive Latin-1 or ASCII re-encode, which is why the case also pins the encoding the specification demands for platform 3.

cases.title: With the editor untouched the English strings are written back, not the German ones
cases.rationale: The fixture’s German name ID 1 deliberately differs from its English one, so this case can tell which record an implementation loaded into its cells. Since the editor reads 3/1/1033 and always writes IDs 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 back, an untouched slice must reproduce the English strings; had it read 3/1/1031 it would write “FixtureNamedInstances Deutsch” into the English record and silently rename the font for English users. The specification’s warning that applications “might display incorrect strings ... if strings for the current platform are not included” is exactly why the localisations must not be conflated.

cases.title: Creating name ID 16 creates one record, not one per platform
cases.rationale: two-axis has Macintosh and Windows English records for IDs 1 to 6 but no ID 16 anywhere, so typing a typographic family name must produce exactly one new record, on the key the editor owns. An implementation that helpfully mirrored the edit onto platform 1 would be inventing data, and would have to encode arbitrary user text in a “platform-specific single- or double-byte encoding” that in general cannot represent it. The set of platform keys in the output must match the set in the input.

cases.title: The output name table is still in the order the specification requires
cases.rationale: The specification is explicit: “name records must be sorted first by platform ID, then by platform-specific encoding ID, then by language ID, and then by name ID.” Editing the table both adds and removes records, and an implementation that appends new ones to the end of the array, or leaves a hole where a removed one was, produces a table that violates that requirement even though every string in it is correct. The case is run on an input that both adds records (17 on the Mac platform is absent, 16 and 17 are rewritten) and removes them (21 and 22 are cleared).

cases.title: Clearing rows 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 leaves five empty records, not five absent ones
cases.rationale: Name IDs 1, 2, 4 and 6 are the strings every platform looks up first, and the specification says fonts “should include all of these strings for the broadest application compatibility”. Deleting them would leave a font that names itself nowhere; writing whatever the user typed, including nothing, at least keeps the required records present and makes the emptiness visible to a validator rather than turning it into a missing record that consumers paper over differently. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 that a zero-length 3/1/1033 record survives a save and reload as a present, empty string.

cases.title: A cleared family-name cell yields a present record whose string is empty
cases.rationale: This is the sharp edge of the empty-versus-absent distinction, isolated on the single most important record. Name ID 1 is “the name the user sees” in the specification’s own worked example, and the rule for IDs 1 to 6 is the opposite of the rule for 16 to 22: the same empty cell means “write an empty string” here and “delete the record” there. A checker must be able to tell the two states apart, so the case asserts both that the record exists and that it is empty.

cases.title: An untouched name editor writes the font's own strings back unchanged
cases.rationale: Because the five mandatory rows are loaded from the font and then always written, doing nothing must be a no-op on those records. Any drift here — a trailing space, a re-encoding, a value picked up from another platform — would mean the editor cannot safely be left alone, which is the property nearly every other case in this area rests on. The expected strings are the ones read out of the fixture with fontTools 4.62.1.

cases.title: Slicing to a different weight does not rewrite the family and subfamily names
cases.rationale: fontTools can regenerate name records from STAT axis values, but only when asked: instantiateVariableFont’s updateFontNames defaults to False and the original does not pass it. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 that pinning wght=1000 leaves name ID 1 saying “Recursive Sans Linear Light” while OS/2.usWeightClass becomes 1000. That mismatch is exactly why a Name Editor exists, and resolving it must stay the user’s decision: the specification’s four-style rule means the right name ID 1 for an ExtraBlack cut is a judgement about family grouping — “the Font Family name for the Arial Black font is Arial Black” — not something a slicer can derive.

cases.title: Non-empty rows 16 and 17 create records on a font that had none
cases.rationale: recursive-vf has no name ID 16 or 17 on any platform, so this exercises creation rather than replacement. The specification recommends exactly this for a sliced family member: “for extended typographic families that includes fonts other than the four basic styles ... it is strongly recommended that name IDs 16 and 17 be used in fonts to create an extended, typographic grouping.” A user pinning one cut out of a five-axis variable font is producing precisely such a member, so the editor must be able to add these records — and must not add 21 and 22, which were left blank.

cases.title: Clearing row 16 deletes the typographic family record and leaves 17, 21 and 22
cases.rationale: For IDs 16, 17, 21 and 22 an empty cell means “this font should not have this record”, and the specification makes absence a defined state with a defined fallback: “if name ID 16 is absent, then name ID 1 is considered to be the typographic family name.” An empty string would instead advertise a typographic family called nothing, which no fallback rescues. The other three records must be untouched, because the user cleared one cell and not four.

cases.title: Clearing the two WWS rows deletes both records and leaves 16 and 17
cases.rationale: IDs 21 and 22 are conditional by design: they are “used to provide a WWS-conformant family name in case the entries for IDs 16 and 17 do not conform to the WWS model”, and the specification adds that “if bit 8 of the OS/2 fsSelection field is set, a WWS Family Name entry should not be needed and should not be included”. A user who slices a font down to a WWS-conformant cut therefore has a real reason to delete them, and the tool must delete rather than blank: an empty ID 21 would still count as “an entry for this ID is included”, which the specification says must correlate with fsSelection bit 8 being clear.

cases.title: Clearing 16, 17, 21 and 22 removes all four when the user asks for it
cases.rationale: This is the output the original produces for every font it touches, but here it is produced because the user deliberately emptied four cells, which makes it correct rather than accidental. The distinction is the whole of D5: the same bytes are right when requested and wrong when imposed. Keeping this case next to the D5 cases makes the corpus say plainly that the deletion mechanism is fine and only its default is not.

cases.title: Deleting the typographic family name removes the 3/1/1033 record only
cases.rationale: The editor’s scope is one localisation, so its deletions are scoped the same way and the German name ID 16 must survive. The result is a table whose English typographic family name is absent while its German one is present — internally odd, but the alternative is a tool that silently deletes localisations the user never saw and cannot restore. Recording the consequence here makes it a deliberate part of the contract rather than an accident, and gives the D5 adjudication the full picture of what scoped deletion produces.

cases.title: Blank rows 16, 17, 21 and 22 on a font that never had them produce nothing
cases.rationale: two-axis has none of the four optional records. Blank cells must therefore be a no-op: not a deletion of something absent, and above all not the creation of four empty records. An empty ID 16 would be worse than none at all, because “if name ID 16 is absent, then name ID 1 is considered to be the typographic family name” — the fallback only fires when the record is genuinely absent.

cases.title: A row containing a single space is written, not treated as cleared
cases.rationale: The boundary between “write it” and “delete it” is an exact comparison against the empty string, so a cell holding one space falls on the write side. Nothing in the name specification forbids a string of whitespace, and the two candidate behaviours differ materially — one output has an ID 16 record and the other does not — so the corpus has to say which. Trimming would be a silent reinterpretation of what the user typed, the same fault the corpus rejects in B8; if a future version wants to refuse whitespace-only input it should refuse it out loud, not guess.

cases.title: The same empty cell leaves an empty record at ID 4 and no record at ID 21
cases.rationale: This case exists to make the empty-versus-absent distinction impossible to miss: two cells are cleared in one run and the outcomes are opposite. ID 4 stays because the full font name is one of the strings the specification says fonts “should include ... for the broadest application compatibility”; ID 21 goes because it is conditional and its absence is a defined state. An implementation that handles the empty string uniformly will fail exactly one of these two checks, which is the diagnosis the case is built to deliver.

cases.title: Slicing without touching the name editor keeps name IDs 16 and 17
cases.rationale: This is the corrected behaviour for the corpus’s largest suspected defect: the original never loads IDs 16, 17, 21 or 22 into the editor, so all four cells are blank, and D4’s rule then deletes all four from every font it touches. The specification makes those records load-bearing for a fixture like this one, which has eight named instances: name ID 1 “should be shared among at most four fonts that differ only in weight or style (italic/oblique)”, whereas name ID 16’s “typographic family grouping doesn’t impose any constraints on the number of faces within it”, and “if name ID 16 is absent, then name ID 1 is considered to be the typographic family name”. Delete 16 and 17 from a family with more than four styles and every face falls back on the four-style ID 1 / ID 2 grouping, so the fifth and later styles can only be style-linked by being split into separate families — which is why the specification warns that applications assuming that grouping “are likely to provide a poor user experience with variable fonts”. The original is expected to fail this case.

cases.title: Slicing without touching the name editor keeps name IDs 21 and 22
cases.rationale: The same defect strips the WWS pair. IDs 21 and 22 are there for a face whose ID 17 “includes qualifiers for some attribute other than weight, width or slope”, and the specification ties them to a bit: “if an entry for this ID is included, bit 8 should not be set”. Deleting ID 21 while leaving fsSelection bit 8 clear leaves a font that is neither declared WWS-conformant nor annotated with a WWS name, so a layout engine has nothing to group it by. The original is expected to fail this case.

cases.title: Editing the family name leaves the typographic and WWS names alone
cases.rationale: This is the shape the defect takes in ordinary use: the user changes one string and four unrelated records vanish. Under the corrected behaviour the four optional rows were loaded with the font’s own values, so writing them back is a no-op and only name ID 1 changes. The specification’s worked examples for extended families set IDs 1, 2, 16, 17, 21 and 22 together as one coherent set; a tool that lets a user retitle a font while silently discarding four of the six is not editing that set, it is truncating it. The original is expected to fail this case.

cases.title: A partial slice that leaves a variable font also keeps 16, 17, 21 and 22
cases.rationale: The defect is in the name editor, not the instancer, so it applies just as much when the output is still variable — and the stakes are higher there, because the specification observes that “variable fonts can include a large number of named instances, each of which will use a shared typographic family name (name ID 16)”. Pinning wdth leaves five wght instances in fvar, and deleting ID 16 would leave all five without the family name they are meant to share. The original is expected to fail this case.

cases.title: Loading 16 and 17 into the editor does not make them read-only
cases.rationale: The fix for D5 is to load all nine rows rather than five; a careless fix that loaded them but then refused to overwrite would trade one defect for another. Name ID 17 “must be unique within a particular typographic family”, so a user slicing a new cut out of a family very often does have to change it. Loading and editing must compose: the loaded value appears in the cell, the typed value wins, and the German record is not dragged along with it.

cases.title: The German typographic names survive, which is what makes the English loss inconsistent
cases.rationale: The original’s deletion is scoped to 3/1/1033, so a font carrying typographic names in more than one language comes out with the English pair missing and the German pair intact. That is diagnostic rather than mitigating: the specification treats the localisations as translations of one logical string, so a table asserting a German typographic family and no English one is self-contradictory, and consumers that fall back across languages may show German to English users. Both implementations should pass this case; it exists so the D5 adjudication sees the whole of what the original produces.

cases.title: A font with no 16, 17, 21 or 22 does not acquire them
cases.rationale: Loading all nine rows means loading four empty ones when the font has no such records, and the correct output then has no such records either. The specification’s Times New Roman example shows a font that legitimately omits all four — “Preferred Family. No name string present, since it is the same as name ID 1” — so inventing them, for instance by copying ID 1 into ID 16, would add claims the font never made. recursive-vf is exactly such a font: its table holds only IDs 0 to 6 and 269 to 414, verified with fontTools 4.62.1.

cases.title: Non-ASCII text typed into a name cell comes back unchanged
cases.rationale: For the key the editor writes, the specification is unambiguous: outside the code-page encodings 3, 4 and 5, “all string data for platform 3 must be encoded in UTF-16BE”, which covers the whole Basic Multilingual Plane, so Latin accents, Greek and CJK are all representable and must survive. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: setting this string on 3/1/1033, saving and reloading returns it unchanged, stored as UTF-16BE. A tool that encoded to Latin-1 or fell back to ASCII would mangle names for most of the world’s scripts.

cases.title: Characters outside the BMP survive as UTF-16 surrogate pairs
cases.rationale: Windows encoding ID 1 is named “Unicode BMP”, but the storage format is UTF-16BE, which encodes supplementary characters as surrogate pairs; verified with fontTools 4.62.1, U+1D11E and U+1F600 are stored as d834 dd1e and d83d de00 and decode back unchanged. What the case tests is that the tool neither truncates at the BMP boundary nor splits a pair, either of which would leave lone surrogates in the string storage and a string no decoder can recover. Whether a font ought to carry such a name is a separate question from whether an editor may silently corrupt what the user typed.

cases.title: A non-ASCII edit is not mirrored onto a Macintosh Roman record
cases.rationale: This is where the single-localisation rule earns its keep. Macintosh platform strings “use platform-specific single- or double-byte encodings according to the specified encoding ID”, and Mac Roman cannot represent most of this string, so any implementation that mirrored the edit onto 1/0/0 would have to corrupt it or fail. The Windows record takes the new text; the Mac record keeps its old text, still in mac_roman.

cases.title: A valid PostScript name is written exactly as typed
cases.rationale: Name ID 6 is the most constrained of the nine: “when translated to ASCII, the name string must be no longer than 63 characters and restricted to the printable ASCII subset, codes 33 to 126, except for the 10 characters ‘[’, ‘]’, ‘(’, ‘)’, ‘{’, ‘}’, ‘<’, ‘>’, ‘/’, ‘%’”. A conforming value must therefore pass through untouched — no case folding, no truncation, no normalisation — because the string “is used to invoke a PostScript language font that corresponds to this OpenType font” and any alteration breaks that lookup.

cases.title: A PostScript name containing a space is written unchanged rather than mangled
cases.rationale: A space is outside the printable-ASCII subset the specification allows for name ID 6, so this input is not conformant — but the editor performs no validation, and of the two available behaviours, “write it as typed” and “quietly rewrite it”, the second is strictly worse: the user ships a name they never chose and never saw. Refusing the job would also be defensible, and if the project adopts that it should be recorded as a new claim in the behaviour map rather than arrived at by one implementation guessing. Until then the contract is verbatim, and complaining about the value is a validator’s job.

cases.title: Pinning every axis drops the name records that only named fvar instances
cases.rationale: With no fvar left, the 64 instance subfamily and PostScript name records reference nothing, and the specification reserves “name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive ... for font-specific names”, so these strings are private to the font and worthless once their referrer is gone. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning MONO=0, CASL=0, wght=400, slnt=0, CRSV=0.5 removes IDs 274 through 401 apart from those still reachable from STAT. The user-facing records at IDs 1 to 6 are untouched by pruning.

cases.title: Exactly sixteen name IDs remain after pinning Recursive to Sans Linear Regular
cases.rationale: The pruning rule is not “drop what nothing references” but “drop the IDs that fvar or STAT referenced before and no longer do”, applied only above 255. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 at MONO=0, CASL=0, wght=400, slnt=0, CRSV=0.5: the survivors are exactly IDs 0 to 6, the five STAT design-axis names 269 to 273, and the four STAT axis values that match the pinned location — 402 Sans, 404 Linear, 406 Regular, 413 Upright. Stating the whole set rather than a few members is what lets the case catch over-pruning and under-pruning with one assertion.

cases.title: Pinning wght=700 keeps only the Bold and Normal value names
cases.rationale: The same rule on the fixture the roster designates for name pruning, where the numbering is small enough to read. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=700, wdth=100 leaves IDs 1 to 6, the two axis names 256 and 257, the STAT weight value 263 Bold, and the STAT width value 274 Normal — which survives despite being flagged elidable, because elision affects how a name is displayed, not whether the axis value matches. All eight instance names and their PostScript names go, as do the Condensed and Expanded value names at 273 and 275.

cases.title: A font with no named instances loses no name records when every axis is pinned
cases.rationale: two-axis declares both axes but no fvar instances, so the only name IDs above 255 are the two axis names, and STAT keeps its design axis records in full (G5) with their AxisNameID intact. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=400, wdth=100 removes fvar and removes not one name record. This is the counterexample to reading G10 as “a full pin strips the name table” — what gets pruned depends entirely on what STAT still points at.

cases.title: The Weight axis name record survives even though wght was pinned away
cases.rationale: This is the subtlety that makes “drop unused” the wrong summary. fvar is gone, so nothing in fvar references name ID 271 Weight any more — but STAT keeps its design axis records in full, and each of those records must carry an AxisNameID, so 271 is still referenced and must stay. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: all five axis-name records, 269 to 273, survive a full pin of recursive-vf. An implementation that pruned by walking fvar alone would delete records STAT still points at, leaving a STAT table with dangling name IDs.

cases.title: Name IDs 255 and below are outside the pruning rule entirely
cases.rationale: The specification partitions the number space: “name IDs 26 to 255, inclusive, are reserved for future standard names. Name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive, are reserved for font-specific names such as those referenced by a font’s layout features.” Only the second range can be private to fvar or STAT, so only it can be pruned; a standard name ID means the same thing to every consumer whether or not a table points at it. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: adding IDs 16, 17, 21 and 22 to recursive-vf and then pinning every axis leaves all four in place, along with 0 and 5 — so any loss of those records is attributable to the name editor and not to the instancer.

cases.title: A partial slice prunes only the instance names whose instances went away
cases.rationale: Pinning MONO, CASL, slnt and CRSV while leaving wght free reduces Recursive’s 64 named instances to the 8 upright Sans Linear ones, and only the other 56 may lose their names. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: IDs 338/339, 346/347 and 394/395 — Sans Linear Light, Sans Linear and Sans Linear ExtraBlack with their PostScript names — survive, while the Mono (274) and Sans Casual (342) instance names are gone. The surviving fvar records must still resolve, since the specification requires an instance’s subfamilyNameID to name “entries in the name table”; recursive-vf carries no layout-feature labels, so on this fixture the stronger statement holds too, that every ID above 255 is reachable from fvar or STAT.

cases.title: A stylistic-set UI label is not pruned, even though fvar and STAT never referenced it
cases.rationale: This is the case that shows the rule is not “drop every name ID nothing in fvar or STAT points at”. The specification reserves “name IDs 256 to 32767, inclusive ... for font-specific names such as those referenced by a font’s layout features”, and a GSUB FeatureParams UINameID is exactly such a reference; fontTools prunes only IDs that were variation-referenced before the operation and are not after, so a label that was never in that set is never a candidate. Deleting it would leave the ss01 feature pointing at nothing and strip the name a user interface shows for the feature. Note that the listed no_dangling_name_ids check would wrongly fail this output, which is why name_references_resolve is proposed above and used here instead.

cases.title: Records written by the editor are not pruned by the instancer that ran before them
cases.rationale: Slicing runs first and the name edits second, so nothing the user typed can be swept away by pruning; the ordering matters because a tool that edited first and instanced second would lose any newly written ID above 255. All nine editable IDs are 255 or below and so are safe either way, but the case fixes the observable end state: after a full pin the edited strings are present and the pruned instance names are still gone. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1 at MONO=1, CASL=1, wght=700, slnt=-15, CRSV=1, where the surviving IDs above 255 are 269 to 273, 403, 409 and 414.

cases.title: STAT axis values dropped by the slice take their name records with them
cases.rationale: STAT axis values whose coordinates fall outside the new limits are dropped (G5), and their ValueNameID records then have no referrer left, so they go too. Verified with fontTools 4.62.1: pinning wght=400 keeps 406 Regular and removes 405 Light, 411 Black and 412 ExtraBlack, while pinning CASL=0 keeps 404 Linear and removes 403 Mono. Keeping them would leave orphaned strings in the file; dropping the wrong ones would leave STAT pointing at a name record that is not there.

cases.title: Editing the name table does not bring back instance names the slice removed
cases.rationale: The complement of the exact-set case: an implementation that rebuilt the name table from the source font in order to apply the user’s edits would restore the 128 instance-name records pruning had just removed, inflating the output and orphaning every one of them. The edits must be applied to the sliced table in place. The surviving set is the one verified with fontTools 4.62.1 for this location, and it must not grow because two cells were typed into.

cases.title: After a partial slice every fvar and STAT name reference still resolves
cases.rationale: Pruning guards against orphaned records; this checks the opposite fault, a live reference to a record that is gone. It is reachable in practice, and this fixture shows how: its default instance record uses subfamilyNameID 2, which the fvar specification explicitly permits — “values of 2 or 17 can be used” — so an instance can point at a name ID the name editor owns, and clearing row 17 on a font that used 17 there would leave fvar pointing at nothing. The case slices partially so that fvar and STAT both survive, and clears the two WWS rows, which nothing references, to establish that a legitimate deletion leaves every reference intact.
